newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Left could ease labour, welfare reforms.
newsitem.headline: French Left could ease labour, welfare reforms.

text.p: New Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin may ironically be better placed than his conservative predecessors to reform France's rigid labour market and costly welfare system, political analysts said on Monday.

Sunday's stunning election result, in which the left swept away Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right government and won a 60-seat parliamentary majority, was interpreted by some commentators, notably in the English-language media, as a vote againt necessary social change.
"The political lesson: forward to the past", was the caustic headline in the International Herald Tribune, a global daily published in France.

"The French responded that, even with 12.8 percent unemployment and darkening prospects, they in effect preferred the example of Sweden 25 years ago, which, for all its great success, is now part of the past," commentator John Vinocur wrote.

But closer examination of the French Socialists' record in office suggests they have broken taboos in the past, ending wage indexation, phasing out price and exchange controls and taming inflation, where conservative predecessors had failed.
And they achieved that while reducing the number of working days lost through strikes to a record low.

The left also modernised the French stock exchange and capital markets and, after an initial two-year blitz of nationalisations and devaluations in 1981-83, embraced the market economy and maintained a stable franc.

Critics of Jospin have focused on two campaign pledges they see as flying in the face of global economic reality -- a plan to create 700,000 jobs, half of them in the public sector, over three years, and a pledge of legislation to reduce the work week from 39 hours to 35 over time without loss of pay.
Yet Jospin has said both measures will be subject to negotiations in a national conference on wages, working hours and jobs which he plans to hold later this year.

Anxious French industrialists have warned against any attempt to twist their arm into conceding uneconomic pay rises or damaging their competitiveness by cutting the working week without any reduction in labour costs.

In a statement on Monday, the CNPF employers' federation said: "Economic policy must reinforce the competitiveness of existing companies, do everything to facilitate the creation of new enterprises and increase growth while respecting financial balances."
Jospin has been careful to stress that he has no intention of overloading small and medium-sized businesses which cannot afford to pay more for less work.

On the contrary, his advisers say, the conference could be a vehicle for binding France's relatively weak trade unions into a negotiation in which organised labour might trade off some greater degree of labour market flexibility against pledges on job creation, shorter hours or longer job-sharing.

"What this country sorely lacks is a social dialogue that can build a consensus on ways to overcome unemployment," said a close Jospin aide. "Juppe's greatest mistake was to try to impose reforms without dialogue, provoking confrontation."
"The national conference is a way of drawing in both employers and unions, of getting them pregnant," he said.

Simultaneously announced plans to streamline the health, pensions and social security system and overhaul the loss-making railways sparked a 24-day public transport strike in late 1995 which forced Juppe to back down on his rail reform and drop proposals to make civil servants work longer for a pension.

One senior French economic policymaker said the French left should look not to the widely-eschewed "Anglo-Saxon model" but to successful efforts by centre-left governments in the Netherlands or Ireland to reduce unemployment without scrapping social protection.

"We are very attached to equality, fraternity and justice in France but I'm convinced the answer to our problems lies in the Dutch model. We could solve many of them by following their consensus solutions," he said.

While right-wing commentators have contrasted Jospin's platform with the market-oriented philosophy of new British Prime Minister Tony Blair, the French left never discarded what Jospin calls its "government culture" while in opposition.

The Socialists' period in the wilderness was too short for them to swing far to the radical left, unlike the German Social Democrats and Britain's Labour Party, which both made themselves virtually unelectable in the 1980s by embracing unilateral nuclear disarmament.
Indeed Jospin's spell in the political wilderness was so short that French wags call it "not so much crossing the desert as crossing the sandpit".
